Plan this as a Rhylthyme protocol and deliver a live timeline: Western Blot: SDS-PAGE, Wet Transfer and Overnight Primary for one 10-lane gel, one membrane
Resource limits: one gel tank, one wet transfer tank, one orbital rocker, one tray at a time, one cold room, one chemiluminescence imager, one operator.
No finishing time was given; finish as early as the work allows.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Western Blot: SDS-PAGE, Wet Transfer and Overnight Primary

One 10-well precast gel is run, wet-transferred to PVDF and probed overnight. The bench has one gel tank, one wet transfer tank, one orbital rocker that takes a single tray, a heat block, a microcentrifuge, a cold room and one chemiluminescence imager. The transfer tank and the rocker are the two things nothing else can share, so the blot moves through them one stage at a time.

Sample preparation
1. Thaw the lysates on ice and normalise them to 2 mg/mL; 15 minutes.
2. Add 4× Laemmli buffer and denature at 95 °C for 5 minutes in the heat block.
3. Spin the tubes for 2 minutes in the microcentrifuge to collect condensate.

Gel
4. Assemble the tank, seat the precast gel and fill with running buffer; 10 minutes.
5. Load 20 µg per lane and 5 µL of protein ladder; 10 minutes. Nothing is loaded until the denatured samples have been spun down.
6. Run at 120 V for 75 minutes, until the dye front reaches the foot of the gel.

Transfer preparation
7. Put a litre of transfer buffer in the cold room an hour before you need it.
8. One hour into the run, wet a PVDF membrane in methanol for 30 seconds and equilibrate it in transfer buffer; 5 minutes.
9. Soak the fibre pads and filter paper in cold transfer buffer; 10 minutes.

Blot
10. Five minutes after the run ends, prise the gel out of the cassette and build the transfer sandwich with no bubbles; 10 minutes.
11. Transfer at 100 V for 60 minutes with an ice pack in the tank.
12. Stain the membrane with Ponceau S, photograph it and rinse it off; 10 minutes.
13. Block in 5 % milk on the rocker for 1 hour at room temperature.
14. Probe with primary antibody overnight in the cold room; 12 to 18 hours.
15. Wash three times for 10 minutes each on the rocker.
16. Probe with HRP-conjugated secondary on the rocker for 1 hour.
17. Wash three times for 10 minutes each on the rocker.

Detection
18. Fifty minutes into the secondary, mix the ECL substrate; 5 minutes.
19. Drain the membrane, apply the substrate and let it work for 5 minutes.
20. Image the blot; 10 minutes of exposures.
21. Quantify the bands against the loading control; 15 minutes.
>>>

A program is made of tracks, where each track is a sequential line and overlapping work must be placed on separate tracks. Each step has exactly one duration kind: fixed, variable, or indefinite. A start trigger specifies whether a step begins at program start, after an offset or predecessor, after a buffered predecessor, manually, on abort, or through a compound condition. Step IDs must be unique across the entire program, and every task used by a step must have a matching resource constraint whose `maxConcurrent` limits simultaneous use. Repeated work belongs on one replicated step with serial, parallel, or staggered instances; subsequent per-instance work uses `instances: "each"`, barriers use `instances: "all"`, and `maxInFlight` limits holding capacity when needed. Turn 4 of 4 — relationships, then the program.

Take the step list from turn 3 exactly as it stands.

**First, tracks.** Put each step in a track: one track per parallel line of work — per dish, per station, per instrument, per performer, per sample group. Steps in one track run one after another and must not overlap; anything that runs while something else runs belongs in its own track.

**Second, triggers.** Give every step a `startTrigger` from this vocabulary and no other:

- `{"type":"programStart"}` — at t = 0.
- `{"type":"programStartOffset","offsetSeconds":n}` — n seconds after the start; this is how a short track is delayed so it finishes with the others.
- `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"x"}` — when x ends. Add `"offsetSeconds"` for a gap, `"event":"start"` to hang off x's start instead of its end, `"instances"` when x is replicated.
- `{"type":"afterStepWithBuffer","stepId":"x","bufferSeconds":n}` — n seconds after x ends.
- `{"type":"manual"}` — the person taps to start it: a gate that no clock can predict (guests seated, dough looks right, the surgeon is ready).
- `{"type":"compound","logic":"all"|"any","triggers":[...]}` — wait for all of, or the first of, several triggers.

**Third, refine the question before you answer it.** Within the scope of scheduling these activities for one person to follow, suggest a better version of the question "which activities depend on which, and which can run at the same time?" — one that would expose dependencies this text implies but does not state: things that must cool, rest, preheat, thaw, proof, be held warm, or be ready at the same moment as something else. Write your improved question out, answer it, and revise the triggers accordingly. A step the improved question reveals is added here, marked `"inferred": true`.

1. If the public catalog already covers this (search_public_recipes or run_protocol), load that instead and stop — its result already has the live URL.
2. Otherwise keep the program you just built; `rhylthyme://guide/authoring` is the cheat-sheet and `rhylthyme://examples/*` are complete programs to pattern-match.
3. Express the limits as constraints, not as copied JSON: the `resourceConstraints`, `replicates`, `instances` and `maxInFlight` you confirmed in turn 2.
4. Run validate_program and fix every error it reports.
5. Run analyze_schedule to check the makespan, critical path and resource conflicts; adjust offsets so tracks finish together. Its `bindingConstraints` say which limit is actually gating the makespan.
6. Call visualize_schedule and give the user the live URL plus the Gantt/itinerary from the result. Do not describe the schedule in prose.
